analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy protections to cover kids up to 16 and mobile apps.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee for the rest of the Congress, backed by just two members, one from each party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the 1998 children's online privacy law. Websites, online services, and mobile apps would need a parent's permission before collecting personal information from children under 16, instead of under 13. Location and biometric data would count as protected personal information, apps on phones and tablets would be covered for the first time, parents could demand that a company delete their child's data, and companies could not cut off service to a child whose parent said no to further data collection. The Federal Trade Commission would also have to study whether the current rule, which only triggers protections when a company actually knows a user is a child, is still the right approach.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 16 and their parents gain: parents would have to consent before companies could collect a child's personal data from websites or apps, would have the right to have that data deleted, and companies could not punish a child for a parent's refusal by terminating service. Families benefit most from extending these rules to mobile apps, which are how most children actually use the internet today, and from treating location tracking and biometric data as sensitive.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the age below which companies must get verifiable parental consent before collecting a child's personal information from under 13 to under 16.
Adds precise geolocation information and biometric information, such as fingerprints, facial patterns, and genetic data, to the categories of personal information protected under the law.
Extends all child privacy protections to mobile applications on phones, tablets, and similar devices, closing a gap in a law written in 1998.

Requires operators to delete a child's personal information upon a verified parent's request and prohibits them from terminating service to a child whose parent refused further collection or use of the child's data.

Directs the Federal Trade Commission to study the 'actual knowledge' standard, under which protections apply only when a company actually knows it is collecting data from a child, and report on whether that standard should change.

analysis.who_pays: Websites, mobile app developers, and the advertising industry that profits from data about minors bear the compliance costs: building parental consent and deletion systems for users under 16, collecting less location and biometric data from children, and forgoing the ability to cut service off to pressure parents. Teens aged 13 to 15 would also need parental permission to use services, which could limit their access to apps and websites.

drawbacks.text: Requiring verifiable parental consent for 13-to-15-year-olds would impose compliance costs on app developers and website operators, a burden that falls hardest on small companies rather than large platforms.

Because the protections trigger only when an operator has 'actual knowledge' a user is a child, the bill leaves that standard in place and merely asks the FTC to study it, so in practice many companies collecting data from minors without knowing it would remain untouched.
Mandating parental consent for teenagers up to 16 can cut teens off from online services, including ones where teens may have reasons to keep their activity private from their parents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are modest and sensible: updating a 1998 law to cover mobile apps, location tracking, and biometric data responds to how children actually use the internet now. The main costs are compliance burdens on smaller developers and the trade-off that teenagers need parental permission to use services. The bill's biggest weakness is that it leaves the weak 'actual knowledge' trigger untouched, so a company can avoid all obligations simply by not knowing its users are children; the bill only commissions a study on that problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee the day after introduction, and no committee ever took it up or voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Walberg introduced the bill on March 10, 2021, with Representative Bobby Rush as the original cosponsor, making it a two-member, two-party effort from the start.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and the next day it went to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a committee vote, never reached the House floor, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms, app developers, and the digital advertising business are better off, because no new restrictions were placed on collecting data from children 13 to 15 or through mobile apps. Families gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online platforms and the ad industry

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand children's online privacy protections on March 10, 2021.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it one supporter from each party.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Frank Pallone
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote or markup; it went to a subcommittee on March 11, 2021 and sat there for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members were ever attached to the bill, one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, so no party bloc or roll call ever weighed in and the partisan shape of any potential vote is unknown.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and online services
industries.note: The bill would force consent, deletion, and no-cutoff rules for collecting data from children under 16, cutting off a source of data these companies monetize. Its death left the existing rules, written for a 1998 internet, in place.
Apps are currently outside the child privacy law; the bill would have brought them under it, requiring parental consent systems for users under 16. The bill died before any of that took effect.

Adding precise geolocation and biometric data to the protected categories, and covering apps, would have restricted the tracking data used to target minors. Nothing in the bill became law, so this data collection continued unchanged.
